Definition: Whether the system enables individuals to authenticate themselves or their documents digitally through electronic verification
Comments: Uganda's NID supports digital authentication via the NIRA Third Party Interface (TPI), which allows real-time biometric (fingerprint) and demographic verification against the NIR. NITA-U operates UGPass, a digital authentication and electronic signature platform using PKI that requires a national ID for onboarding. The NID is used for e-KYC across 74+ financial institutions. MOSIP-based authentication is being deployed as part of the 2024–2026 system upgrade.

Definition: Whether authentication is possible through a centralized government portal or digital gateway
Comments: Uganda's e-government portal (ecitizen.go.ug) and digital services require NIN/NID for authentication. NITA-U's UGPass platform provides digital authentication for government portals using the National ID. The e-GIF framework establishes a centralised government authentication gateway. NIRA's online pre-registration portal launched in 2024/2025 also uses NIN-based authentication. The NID is required for portal access to services like URA (tax), NSSF, and education portals.

Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: Under the Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019, data subjects have the right to access, rectify, and request erasure of their personal data. NIRA's online self-registration portal (launched 2025) allows citizens to view and update their registration details. Citizens can request corrections to ID data (at a cost of USh 200,000 for non-NIRA errors). The DPPA gives individuals the right to request their personal data from any data controller.

Definition: Whether the system enables Know Your Customer (KYC) packet collection for service provision, particularly financial services
Comments: Uganda has a robust e-KYC system built on the NIRA database. The Bank of Uganda reports 74 financial institutions (commercial banks, MFIs, fintechs, insurance, telecoms) have access to NIRA's database for digital KYC as of 2024. The E-KYC project (FSD Uganda, BOU, NIRA) enables real-time identity verification using NIN, card number, name, and date of birth. The Bank of Uganda issued a directive in April 2024 requiring ID verification for all transactions above UGX 1 million.

Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: Uganda's general court system exercises judicial oversight over the national ID system, but no ID-specific judicial mechanisms exist. The High Court heard and dismissed (June 2025) a civil suit challenging mandatory NID requirements for accessing social services (ISER & 2 Others v Attorney General & NIRA). Courts have adjudicated ID-related disputes (election petitions, cancellation orders under ROPA s.57). There is no specialised tribunal for identity disputes.

Definition: Whether the civil registration and digital ID systems are integrated
Comments: NIRA is mandated under ROPA 2015 to register births, deaths, and adoptions and link them to the NIR. The MOSIP-OpenCRVS integration project (2025) aims to link birth registrations to instant NIN creation. However, integration is only partial: birth registration coverage is ~32% and death registration ~2%, creating gaps in the NIR. The Mobile Vital Registration System (MVRS) operates in 112/135 districts. Full integration is underway but not yet complete.

Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: Data sharing rules exist but are only partially defined. The ROPA 2015 (Section 65) specifies permitted uses of NIR data (security, taxation, health, social services, immigration etc.) and NIRA controls TPI access for third parties. The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 sets consent and purpose-limitation rules for data sharing. However, civil society has raised concerns about inadequate safeguards and opaque data sharing with security agencies.

Definition: Whether specific regulation or policy addresses digital ID beyond general identification legislation
Comments: The Registration of Persons Act 2015 is a dedicated legal instrument specifically governing Uganda's digital/biometric national ID system, establishing NIRA, the NIR, biometric enrollment requirements, mandatory card use, and data management rules. This constitutes digital ID-specific regulation beyond general e-government law.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: Uganda enacted the Data Protection and Privacy Act (DPPA) No. 9 of 2019, which regulates the collection, processing, and use of personal data including biometric data in the national ID system. The Act establishes seven data protection principles, data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure), consent requirements, and breach notification obligations.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 establishes the Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO) under NITA-U, headed by a National Personal Data Protection Director. The PDPO is mandated to enforce the DPPA, investigate complaints, conduct audits, maintain a data protection register, and supervise data collectors and processors. The PDPO recorded its first-ever criminal conviction under the DPPA in July 2025.

Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: Under Section 69 of the Registration of Persons Act 2015, the national identification card is prima facie proof of the particulars contained in it, including citizenship. The NIN serves as legal proof of identity for accessing services including banking, SIM registration, health, education, elections, and property transactions. The High Court upheld the legality of using the NID as the primary identification instrument.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: Uganda has a comprehensive legal framework for its national ID system. The Registration of Persons Act (ROPA) 2015 (Cap. 332) establishes NIRA, the NIR, and mandates compulsory registration of citizens and alien residents. It sets out data use, mandatory use of national ID cards for services (Section 66), and offences. The system was originally launched under the National Security Information System (NSIS) in 2014.

Definition: Whether the system and the production of credentials can be managed, maintained and developed by in-country technical staff (as opposed to foreign vendors)
Comments: NIRA is the government authority responsible for the NIR, but significant technology components rely on foreign vendors. The original NSIS used Muehlbauer High Tech International equipment; the 2024–2026 upgrade contracts involved Veridos and Tahaluf (Abu Dhabi) with Technoforte (India) as system integrator for MOSIP/OpenCRVS. IriTech (South Korea/USA) provides iris biometric technology. There is partial in-country capacity (NIRA staff, data centres in Uganda), but core technology and card production remain vendor-dependent.

Definition: Whether the Ministry of Finance has oversight of the financing and development of the digital ID system
Comments: NIRA is funded through the national budget under the Ministry of Internal Affairs (Vote 137), with the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED) overseeing budget allocations. The 2022/23–2026/27 MTEF shows USh 65.5 billion annually allocated to NIRA. The mass enrollment exercise (USh 666.85 billion) was Cabinet-approved and Treasury-funded. MoFPED has oversight through the budget cycle but oversight is partial given documented underfunding.

Definition: Whether the ongoing management, maintenance and development of the ID system can be funded by sustainable domestic resources
Comments: Uganda's ID system is funded through a mix of domestic government budget (GoU) and external financing. The mass enrollment exercise (USh 666.85B) is primarily domestically funded via the national budget. NIRA's regular annual budget (USh 65.5B) is from domestic GoU sources. However, the World Bank ID4D diagnostic noted significant underfunding (only ~43% of needs met domestically). Past system development involved World Bank loans and UNICEF support. The new MOSIP implementation involves external technical partnerships.

Definition: Whether the system collects biometric data and which modalities are collected (fingerprints, facial image, iris scans)
Comments: The 2024–2026 mass enrollment exercise introduced iris biometrics (IriTech IriShield BK scanners) in addition to fingerprints and facial images that were already collected. NIRA has migrated 28 million biometric records to the MOSIP platform. The new registration kits collect fingerprints, iris scans, and face images. Iris biometrics were added to address the ~1 million fingerprint records that had degraded.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: The National Identification Register (NIR) is maintained as a fully digital centralised database. NIRA has migrated 28–30 million biometric records to the MOSIP open-source identity platform. The registration system uses digital biometric kits, a web-based MVRS for civil registration, and a central data centre. The Registration of Persons Act 2015 mandates the register be maintained as an electronic database.

Definition: Whether the country has established or is actively developing a national digital identity system, including foundational ID systems that enable authentication across multiple services. Fully deployed means operational nationwide and accepting new registrations.
Comments: Uganda's National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA) operates a fully deployed nationwide biometric digital ID system (Ndaga Muntu/NID), established under the Registration of Persons Act 2015. Over 27.4 million persons are registered in the National Identification Register as of October 2024, with mass enrollment ongoing (2024–2026 exercise targeting 17.2 million new registrants and 15.8 million renewals). The system is deployed at parish level across all 135 districts and 11 cities.

Definition: Whether the digital ID system is designed to be interoperable across government agencies and with other systems through APIs or data exchange protocols
Comments: NIRA's National Identification Register is integrated with 95+ institutions (banks, telecoms, government agencies) via a Third Party Interface (TPI) for real-time identity verification. Uganda has published an e-Government Interoperability Framework (e-GIF) via NITA-U. MOSIP's modular design supports interoperability with OpenCRVS and other systems. The NID is used as primary identifier across government services (URA, NSSF, electoral commission, health, education).

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for opening bank accounts and accessing financial services
Comments: The national ID is mandatory for banking and financial services. The Registration of Persons Act 2015 (Section 66) mandates NID for financial services. The Bank of Uganda issued a directive in April 2024 requiring NID verification for all transactions above UGX 1 million. Citizens without NID are denied bank account opening. 74 financial institutions are connected to NIRA's database for mandatory e-KYC. NIRA and the Uganda Bankers Association have formalised this requirement.

Definition: Whether credentials are issued free of charge
Comments: The national ID credential is not free for all. First-time adult registration and standard renewals are free (during the mass enrollment exercise). However, replacement of a lost ID costs USh 50,000 (~$13.50), and corrections/updates to records cost USh 200,000 (~$54). Alien IDs cost approximately US$100. These fees create cost barriers for vulnerable populations.

Definition: Whether the digital ID is recognized or interoperable across borders through regional agreements or travel documents
Value Name: Recognized in some regional contexts (e.g., ECOWAS travel)
Comments: Uganda's national ID is formally recognised as a travel document for cross-border movement within the East African Community (EAC), specifically between Uganda, Kenya, and Rwanda under the Northern Corridor Integration Projects (NCIP) agreement from January 2014. Citizens of these three countries can cross each other's borders using national IDs in lieu of passports. Tanzania does not participate as it lacks a national ID system. This constitutes formal regional interoperability among some EAC states.

Definition: Age in years at which an individual becomes eligible to register for digital ID
Comments: The national ID card (Ndaga Muntu) is issued to citizens aged 16 and above. NINs are assigned to children from birth (via civil registration) and school-going learners aged 5+ (via the Learners Project). However, the physical ID card is only issued from age 16. This places the enrollment eligibility for the physical credential at 16–17 years (>17 bracket does not apply; the 10–17 bracket best fits as cards are issued at 16).

Definition: Whether registration for digital ID is mandatory, optional, or mandatory for specific groups
Comments: Registration is compulsory for all citizens and legal alien residents under Part VIII of the Registration of Persons Act 2015 (Section 54: 'Compulsory registration'). The NID is mandatory for accessing a wide range of services including SIM registration, banking, health, education, social services, passports, and voter registration. The High Court in June 2025 upheld the mandatory use of NID for accessing services.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for accessing public healthcare services
Comments: The national ID is mandatory for accessing healthcare in Uganda. Pregnant women without NID have been turned away from health centres; citizens without NID are denied access to National Health System services. CIPESA (2023) and civil society organisations documented unregistered individuals being denied healthcare. The mandatory NID requirement was challenged in the High Court by ISER and others, but upheld in June 2025.

Definition: Whether non-nationals including refugees, asylum seekers, and permanent residents are eligible to register
Comments: Legal alien residents (with valid permits/passes under the Uganda Citizenship and Immigration Control Act) are eligible for Alien Identification Numbers (AIN) and Alien ID cards under ROPA 2015 (Sections 72–74). However, refugees recognised by the government and UNHCR are explicitly excluded from ROPA (Section 1(2)(b)) and are managed separately by the Office of the Prime Minister. Thus only some non-nationals (legal residents but not refugees) are eligible.

Definition: Percentage of eligible population that has been issued or registered with digital ID credentials
Comments: As of October 2024, 27.4 million persons are registered in the NIR out of a total population of approximately 45.9 million, equating to about 60% of total population. The World Bank ID4D diagnostic (2019) estimated 66% coverage at that time. Coverage of those 16+ is higher (~90% per 2015 data). An estimated 17.2 million remain unregistered as of 2024 per NIRA. This places coverage in the 50–69% range nationally.

Definition: Whether ID system undergoes regular security audits, penetration testing, or vulnerability assessments
Comments: Uganda's NID system incorporates security features including polycarbonate card with laser engraving, UV ink, ICAO MRZ, 2D barcode with embedded fingerprint, and AFIS deduplication. IriTech's iris scanners underwent NIST testing and obtained MOSIP MACP Framework certification (BixeLab). Internal audit functions are built into NIRA's budget framework. However, a 2017 data breach was alleged (denied by government). Civil society has called for formal independent security audits. The World Bank ID4D diagnostic recommended formal cybersecurity audits and SOC establishment.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for SIM card activation and mobile service registration
Comments: SIM card registration requiring a national ID is mandatory in Uganda. The Registration of Persons Act 2015 (Section 66) mandated NID for SIM card registration. This was enforced starting 2017, with all five mobile network operators (MNOs) connected to NIRA's TPI for biometric SIM verification. Citizens without an NID cannot register a SIM card. CIPESA and Yale Law School have documented this mandatory requirement and its exclusionary effects.
